about: Every source of the flame test lab's record (docs/research/flame/flame.json) and of its primer (src/chem-data/flame/primer.ts), each fetched and read on the retrieval date for this lab, where the work was done; by the clock in UTC some of the requests fall in the first hours of 2026-10-09, and the citation of the one kept response gives its time so. A source with `file` has its copy in this folder, as returned, with the sha256 of that copy; a source with none was read and no copy is kept. `fetchedSha256`, on a source with no copy, is the sha256 of the file as it was fetched: a record of which file was read, not the hash of anything here, and nothing checks it. Each `supports` row names in `fields` the stored values it supports, each by its place in the record with the item's id in brackets (salts[cacl2-0.1m].features[caoh-green], salts[kcl-0.1m].notes[0], closing.answer); gives in `prints` a figure, a formula, a label or a heading exactly as the source prints it; and says in `where`, in this project's words, where that is, what the source says there, and how far the stored value goes beyond it. A row whose field is `primer` marks a source the primer rests on. The build holds the record to these rows: every source a value cites must have a row that names the value, and where the record stores the figure a source prints, a row for it must print that figure. No source is quoted beyond such figures, formulas, labels and headings. Two sources are also listed by other manifests and are written here exactly as they are there, so that the build lists each once: the saved tables of the emission spectra (docs/research/emission-spectra/sources/), and the six safety data sheets for the solutions, which are also in sources/hazard-manifest.json for the notes under the bottles' hazards. The hazard statements and those notes are not in this file: they are in hazards.json and sources/hazard-manifest.json, which the build merges in. README.md, one folder up, says what could not be sourced.

The same row prints the relative intensity 18, the larger of the pair, which is why this line stands for the pair. It is smaller than the 25 and 24 that the table of 700 to 780 nm prints for the deep red pair, and the violet pair is ranked after the red one on that ground; NIST calls its intensities qualitative.
The saved table docs/research/emission-spectra/sources/nist-asd-lines-k.txt, column obs_wl_air(nm). The next row of the table, 0.31 nm away, with the relative intensity 17.

The saved table docs/research/emission-spectra/sources/nist-asd-lines-na.txt, column obs_wl_air(nm). The same row prints the relative intensity 80000, the larger of the two, which is why this line stands for the pair.
The saved table docs/research/emission-spectra/sources/nist-asd-lines-na.txt, column obs_wl_air(nm). The next row of the table, 0.60 nm away, with the relative intensity 40000.
The saved table docs/research/emission-spectra/sources/nist-asd-lines-sr.txt, column obs_wl_air(nm). The same row prints the relative intensity 29000r.
The heading of the column each of these notes takes its wavelength from, rounded to a tenth of a nanometre: 553.5481, 422.673, 460.7331, and 588.995095 with 589.592424.

The column the periodic table's card for this element takes its lines from, in the saved table of the neutral atom between 400 and 700 nm. The note says what that card shows; which lines the card picks is the rule of docs/research/emission-spectra/README.md. For potassium the saved table holds 404.4136 and 404.7208 and nothing beyond 700 nm; for sodium it holds 588.995095 and 589.592424. That the flame is not the colour of those lines is this lab's own conclusion from its other sources.

sources.citation: Human, H. G. C.; Zeegers, P. J. Th. Molecular fluorescence of CaOH, SrOH and BaCl in flames. Spectrochimica Acta Part B 1975, 30, 203-209. Read as the scanned copy in the Utrecht University Repository, linked here, whose pages were turned into images and read by eye; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-08).

supports.where: Section 3.1, Spectra obtained: the maxima of the two main bands of CaOH in the flame, a flame of hydrogen and oxygen in argon into which a solution of the salt was sprayed. Figure 1, the emission spectrum on a scale of 5500 to 6600 Å, draws the band at 6230 Å about twice as tall as the one at 5540 Å and much wider; the orange-red band is ranked first on that ground. The figure is not corrected for how the instrument or the eye responds to each colour. The limits of the two bands are the other source's.
Section 3.1: two further maxima, which the paper takes to belong with the band at 6230 Å. Figure 1 draws them much lower than it.

The paper's title and its section 3.1: the bands that make up the calcium spectrum of the flame are the molecule's. That the flame is therefore not the colour of the atom's lines is this lab's own conclusion.

Section 3.2 and the heading of Table 2: the bandhead of SrOH at the long end. Figure 2, the emission spectrum on a scale of 6000 to 7000 Å, draws this the tallest thing in the strontium spectrum, with a second maximum near 6720 Å about three quarters as tall and the band at 6060 Å about half as tall; the red band is ranked first on that ground, with the same caution as for calcium. The paper gives no limits. The stored band runs from 671 nm, the other source's shortest position, to this bandhead, and is marked approximate.
Section 3.2 and the heading of Table 2: the other bandhead of SrOH. No limits are given, and the band is stored at this one position and marked approximate.

The paper's title and Figure 2: the bands that make up the strontium spectrum of the flame are the molecule's. That the flame is therefore not the colour of the atom's lines is this lab's own conclusion.
Section 3.1, after Figure 3: the maxima of the green bands of BaOH, which the paper says emit strongly in the flame and could not be made to fluoresce. The limits of the band are the other source's.

The paper's first sentence, as its scan reads: the line at which barium atoms are measured in flames, which the bands of CaOH near 5540 Å get in the way of. The paper measures the line by the light the atoms take up, not by the light they give; that the atom's line is on the strip beside the band, and ranked after it, rests on this and on nothing more. Its wavelength is NIST's.
Section 3.1, across the foot of the page with Figure 2 and the head of the next: the limits between which the bands of BaO lie, named with the green bands of BaOH as emitting strongly in the flame.

Figure 3, the spectrum of BaCl when a solution of barium chloride is sprayed into the flame, whose peaks are labelled in ångströms and called approximate: 5136 and 5241 are the two tall ones, with 5168, 5207 and 5320 between and beyond. A footnote calls the bands narrow beside those of CaOH and SrOH. The spectrum drawn is of fluorescence; the abstract says that fluorescence and emission spectra were the same.

supports.prints: Molecular fluorescence of CaOH, SrOH and BaCl in flames
supports.where: The paper's title. Read at its abstract, its introduction, section 3.1 with Figures 1 to 3, and section 3.2 as far as Table 2.

supports.where: The abstract: the second of the two ranges of wavelength in which the spectra of CaOH were measured, for solutions of calcium chloride and of calcium nitrate in a flame of air and acetylene. It is stored as the limits of the orange-red band. The abstract does not say that the molecule gives no light outside the range, and it says which band took up light the more strongly, not which gave the more.
The abstract: the first of the two ranges, stored as the limits of the green band. The abstract says that the spectrum at 554 nm was taken up strongly.

The abstract: the atom's line was measured in the same flame beside the bands of the molecules. The abstract does not give its wavelength, which is NIST's, and it measures the line by the light the atoms take up; that the line is on the strip, and ranked last, rests on this and on nothing more.

sources.citation: Kirchhoff, G.; Bunsen, R. Chemical Analysis by Observation of Spectra. Annalen der Physik und der Chemie (Poggendorff) 1860, 110, 161-189. Read in an abridged English translation, with no translator named, on the ChemTeam's page of classic papers, linked here; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-08).

supports.where: Under Potassium: what the flame of a potassium compound shows in a spectroscope, one line at the far red end, at the edge of the infrared, and one far in the violet. The authors held a bead of the chloride in the flame of a gas burner. The wavelengths are NIST's.
Under Potassium: beside its two lines the flame gives a long spectrum with no lines in it.

Under Strontium: the last of the eight lines the authors call very prominent, six of them red and one orange. The blue one is taken to be the atom's line that NIST lists at 460.7331 nm; the translation gives no wavelength. The lab stores one red band where the authors count six red lines.
Under Sodium: what the flame showed in the spectroscope when a little of a sodium salt was in the air of the room, with the flame turned yellow.

Under Lithium: with a bead that holds a little lithium salt and much sodium salt in the flame, the eye alone sees sodium's colour and none of lithium's red, while the spectroscope shows the red line of lithium beside the line of sodium. The lab takes this to hold for each of its other five salts; the passage is about lithium.

Before the section on sodium: the authors compared the chlorides with five other kinds of compound of the same metals (bromides and iodides, oxides, carbonates, sulphates), in flames of several kinds, and found the lines of each metal in the same places whatever the compound. So what a flame's spectrum shows belongs to the metal and not to what it was combined with.

supports.prints: Chemical Analysis by Observation of Spectra
supports.where: The paper's title. Read whole, as far as the translation goes: the description of the apparatus and the sections on sodium, lithium, potassium, strontium, calcium and barium.

sources.citation: Juknelevičius, D. Illuminating pyrotechnic compositions and their specific features. Doctoral dissertation, Vilnius University, 2020. https://doi.org/10.15388/vu.thesis.122. Read in the repository of the university, linked here, with a paper it reprints: Juknelevicius, D.; Dufter, A.; Rusan, M.; Klapötke, T. M.; Ramanavicius, A. Study of Pyrotechnic Blue Strobe Compositions Based on Ammonium Perchlorate and Tetramethylammonium Nitrate. Eur. J. Inorg. Chem. 2017, 1113-1119; read and not kept (retrieved 2026-10-08).

supports.where: Section 3.5, Blue illuminants: where the strong light of CuCl lies in the spectra of the blue mixtures. The reprinted paper, under Emission Spectra, puts the light of copper(I) chloride in the region of 400 to 500 nm and calls it the dominating one. Both are about firework mixtures that hold a source of chlorine, burnt as pellets, and not about a solution of copper(II) chloride on a loop in a burner's flame: that the blue band is the brightest thing at this station rests on taking the one for the other.

The reprinted paper, under Emission Spectra: the region where copper hydroxide gives one wide band, overlapping the light of the chloride. Section 3.7 of the dissertation calls a green flame the light of CuOH. No limits are given, and the band is stored at this one position and marked approximate.
The reprinted paper, under Emission Spectra: what copper oxide gives, in the red, with no wavelength.

The heading in the reprinted paper. Under it the spectra of the copper mixtures are said to hold the light of the chloride, the hydroxide and the oxide of copper and the lines of sodium and potassium that are there as impurities; no line of the copper atom is named. That is the ground for storing none. It is an absence in one source and not a measurement.
The reprinted paper, under Emission Spectra: the sharp line that potassium gives in a flame, there as an impurity. Section 3.5 of the dissertation notes that this light is outside what the eye sees.

Section 3.1 of the dissertation: a source of chlorine in a strontium mixture raises the light of this molecule, which adds to that of SrOH and moves the flame's colour from a reddish orange to red. Section 3.4 says that with no chlorine the spectrum is that of SrOH with lines of sodium and potassium. Neither gives a wavelength for SrCl.

supports.prints: Illuminating pyrotechnic compositions and their specific features
supports.where: The dissertation's title. Read at its sections 1.3, 3.1, 3.4, 3.5 and 3.7 and, in the reprinted paper, under Emission Spectra.
